description: Coyote offers to help find Myra's missing eye, searches among vegetation and rocks, and then abandons the search.
outcome: The search is abandoned without finding the eye.
evidence_excerpt: The coyote was trotting busily around, nosing under clumps of rabbit-brush and cheat-grass, pawing at a rock. "Aren't you going to look?" it said, suddenly sitting down on its haunches and abandoning the search.
notes: Records an attempted act of help; the text does not establish successful recovery.

description: Myra follows Coyote down the gulley to a creek, where they both drink.
outcome: Both reach the creek and drink.
location: Gulley and creek below the rimrock
evidence_excerpt: After a while the coyote slanted down the undercut slope and the child scrambled after, through scrub willows to the thin creek in its wide sandbed. Both drank.
notes: Guidance is the dataset category; the passage shows Myra following rather than an explicit agreement to guide her.

description: Coyote licks and cleans Myra's injured eye area after Myra struggles to remove her blood-stuck hand. Myra holds and strokes Coyote.
outcome: Myra cries a little with relief and feels comforted.
evidence_excerpt: It began to lick the awful, aching blindness, cleaning and cleaning with its curled, precise, strong, wet tongue, until the child was able to cry a little with relief, being comforted.
notes: Source line-break hyphenation in 'cleaning' is joined.

description: Coyote invites Myra to eat. They share dried salmon mush, initially using twigs, then fingers; Myra practices the eating technique.
outcome: They eat in turns until only the rocks remain in the pot.
resources: dried salmon mush; pot-basket; sagebrush twigs; rocks
evidence_excerpt: The child, when she tried, got mush all over her chin. It was like chopsticks, it took practice. She practiced. They ate turn and turn until nothing was left in the pot but three rocks.
notes: The material is named by Coyote as dried salmon mush. The scene also presents a different perceived appearance of the meal; it is not assigned a separate biological identity.

description: When Myra wants to go back after remembering the plane, Coyote questions the idea and continues walking faster. Myra protests again but follows.
outcome: Myra continues traveling with Coyote.
evidence_excerpt: The child cried, "I ought to go back —" "What for?" said Coyote. She stopped to look round at the child, then went on faster.
notes: Category describes the expressed disagreement.

description: Several townspeople come to meet Myra, and some of the women help her stand and walk while encouraging her.
outcome: Myra receives physical assistance toward the houses.
evidence_excerpt: Some of the women helped her stand up and walk, coaxing her, "It isn't much farther, you're doing fine."
notes: The helpers are not individually named in this passage.

description: After Young Owl suggests Coyote's house, Chipmunk objects that it is lonely and offers her own household. She takes Myra to the house.
outcome: Myra enters Chipmunk's household.
evidence_excerpt: "She can come with us." That seemed to decide it. The fat-cheeked woman patted the child's arm and took her past several shacks and shanties to a low, windowless house.
notes: The woman is identified as Chipmunk later on the same page.

description: Myra is given food after arriving in the household and eats a little while still unwell.
outcome: Myra eats a little.
evidence_excerpt: The child was given food, and ate a little, but her head swam and the blackness in her right eye kept coming across her left eye so she could not see at all for a while.
notes: The giver and the food are not specified. The nearby comparison to a toasted-sesame smell does not identify the meal as sesame.

description: After Myra asks where she can sleep, a daughter takes her to the back room and invites her onto a sleeping shelf.
outcome: Myra climbs onto a shelf under a blanket and lies down.
evidence_excerpt: "Crawl in!" said Chipmunk's daughter, patting the child's arm in the comforting way they had. The child climbed onto a shelf, under a blanket She laid down her head.
notes: The daughter has no individual name in this passage.

description: The two women wash Myra, clean around her injured eye gently, dry and dress her, braid her hair, and prepare her for the gathering.
outcome: Myra is washed and dressed and accompanies the women to the gathering.
evidence_excerpt: sluiced the child down, washed and stroked her limbs and hands and hair, cleaned around the cheekbone and eyebrow of her right eye with infinite softness, admired her, sudsed her, rinsed her
notes: The action continues onto PDF p. 5, where the women are greeted as Chipmunk and Whitefoot.

description: Jay leads Myra to a mat, tells her to stay still, reassures her about her eye, and organizes the people gathering around her.
outcome: Myra remains seated while the gathering is organized.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: Every now and then Jay rushed over to her and said something like, "Going to be as good as new!" and went off again to organize people, waving his long blue arms and shouting.
notes: Healing is the event's stated purpose; this row records organization and reassurance rather than its later result.

description: Chipmunk, Whitefoot, and their families give Myra reassuring winks while she sits at the gathering.
outcome: Myra gets over the feeling that everyone is staring at her.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: She soon got over feeling that everybody was looking at her, since nobody paid her more attention than a checking glance or, from Chipmunk or Whitefoot and their families, a reassuring wink.
notes: The narration connects her easing self-consciousness with the crowd's limited attention, including the winks; it does not isolate one cause.

description: The Rattler dances around Myra and shakes a rattle while people around the circle sing in time. Myra initially flinches, then sits still.
outcome: Myra remains in the circle as the dancing and singing continue.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: People were singing around the circle now, a few notes repeated in time to the rattle, soft and tuneless. It was exciting and boring, strange and familiar. The Rattler wove his dancing closer and closer to her, darting at her.
notes: Collective performance during Myra's healing gathering.

description: Jay works on Myra's injured eye during the gathering and fits a replacement that he identifies as pine pitch. He asks her to open her eyes and report whether it works.
outcome: Using both eyes, Myra sees blurry, yellowish images with depth; using the uninjured eye alone gives a clear, flat view.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: if she shut the hurting eye and looked with the other, everything was clear and flat; if she used them both, things were blurry and yellowish, but deep.
notes: The eye's material is Jay's statement on the same page.

description: Coyote questions whether Jay used one of her stolen eyes, then mocks his claim to be a doctor and the appearance of the replacement. Jay angrily identifies the material and defends his work.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: "It's pine pitch," Jay shouted furiously. "You think I'd use some stupid secondhand coyote eye? I'm a doctor!" "Ooooh, ooooh, a doctor," Coyote said.
notes: Coyote's reference to stolen eyes is an accusation within dialogue, not independently verified history.

description: After Jay's treatment, Coyote licks across Myra's painful eye area.
outcome: Myra opens both eyes and says the eye works fine.
location: Open gathering place among the houses
evidence_excerpt: the thin, firm tongue once more licked accurate across the pain, cooling clearing When the child opened both eyes again the world looked pretty good. "It works fine," she said.

description: Doe asks where Myra will stay, comments on Coyote's absence, and mentions Chipmunk, Rabbit, and Jackrabbit as possible households.
outcome: Myra says she would prefer to stay with Coyote.
evidence_excerpt: "She isn't home much," the soft-voiced woman said. "You were staying with Chipmunk, weren't you? Or there's Rabbit, or Jackrabbit, they have families..."
notes: Records proposed lodging options; this passage does not show Myra moving into Rabbit's or Jackrabbit's household.

description: Doe accepts Myra's preference and walks beside her to Coyote's cabin, then calls out to check for Coyote.
outcome: They reach Bide-A-Wee; Coyote does not respond.
evidence_excerpt: "OK, that's fine. Her house is over here." Doe walked along beside the child to a ramshackle cabin on the high edge of town.
notes: No explicit invitation from Coyote is recorded in this scene.

description: Before returning to her fawns, Doe checks whether Myra will be all right and says that others in the town will give her food.
outcome: Myra says she is fine and thanks Doe.
evidence_excerpt: "You going to be OK? Anybody else here will give you something to eat—you know... OK?" "Yeah. I'm fine. Thank you," the child said.
notes: This is Doe's statement about available support, not a completed food transfer. Source line-break hyphenation in 'something' is joined.

description: During their conversation, Coyote asks how Myra's injured eye is doing.
outcome: Myra says that her eye is fine.
evidence_excerpt: "Resemblance is in the eye," Coyote said. "How is that lousy eye, by the way?" "It's fine.
notes: The outcome is Myra's own report, not an independent assessment of her eye. The exact spot around the house is unstated.

description: Coyote notices a tick on Myra's collar, removes it, bites it, and spits out the pieces.
outcome: The tick is removed from Myra's collar.
evidence_excerpt: "Hey, that's a tick on your collar." She reached over, flicked the tick off, picked it up on one finger, bit it, and spat out the bits.
notes: The text identifies a tick on clothing; it does not say the tick had bitten Myra.

description: In response to Myra's questions, Coyote explains that different beings see Myra differently, including Coyote's own view of her as a four-legged being.
evidence_excerpt: "So, to me you're basically greyish yellow and run on four legs.
notes: Preserves Coyote as the speaker. Her descriptions of what others see are reported claims, not separate observed transformations.

description: Myra learns to spend the night with Chipmunk or the Rabbits when Coyote's boyfriends visit.
outcome: Myra stays overnight with other households on those occasions.
evidence_excerpt: When her boyfriends came to visit, the child learned to go stay with Chipmunk or the Rabbits for the night
notes: The narration describes a recurring response, without dates, a fixed schedule, or a separately narrated invitation.

description: Coyote intervenes when a visiting friend touches Myra inappropriately, bites him, removes him from the bed, and expels him from the house the next morning.
outcome: The visitor spends the night on the floor and is expelled the next morning. The narration says he visits again later.
evidence_excerpt: Coyote woke up and realized what he was doing bit him hard, and kicked him out of bed. He spent the night on the floor, and apologized next morning
notes: Later in the same page Coyote identifies this visitor as her son; the record does not imply a permanent ban.

description: While Coyote naps, Myra gathers and buries Coyote's dried excrement. Coyote later searches for it, hears it call to her, digs it out, and talks with it.
outcome: Coyote retrieves what Myra buried.
evidence_excerpt: The child gathered up all the old dry turds from around the house one day while Coyote was having a nap, and buried them in a sandy place
notes: The speaking excrement is part of the narrated fictional event. The conflict category describes the disagreement over this household action.

description: Myra apologizes for burying Coyote's excrement and explains that she kept stepping on it. Coyote explains that keeping it nearby is easier for her.
outcome: Both explain their reasons; the text does not state an agreed household rule.
evidence_excerpt: "I'm sorry I did that" "It's just easier when they're all around close by," Coyote said, washing her hands
notes: Repair is an editorial label for the apology. Acceptance of the apology and any change in trust are unstated.

description: The Skunk children make audible remarks about Myra's smell in a passage describing her exclusion by some residents.
evidence_excerpt: Some persons in town made it clear that as far as they were concerned she didn't and never would belong there. Hawk's furious stare burned through her; the Skunk children made audible remarks about what she smelled like.
notes: The exact remarks and their frequency are unstated. The passage gives a general account of treatment in town; repetition is not explicit.

description: Myra and Horned Toad Child dig and build together and play at hunting, gathering, keeping house, and holding dances.
outcome: Horned Toad Child is described as Myra's constant playmate and a loyal friend.
evidence_excerpt: They dug and built together, out among the sagebrush, and played at hunting and gathering and keeping house and holding dances, all the great games.
notes: The activities are explicitly play. They should not be counted as actual hunting, gathering, household labor, or ceremonial dances.

description: When Myra asks where her people live, Horned Toad Child advises her to ask Horse and tells her that Horse often stays near the butte.
outcome: Myra follows the advice and travels to the butte to find Horse.
evidence_excerpt: "Ask Horse," said Horned Toad Child, sagaciously. He had moved away from the water, which he did not like and never drank, and was plaiting rushes.
notes: His further explanation of Horse's history includes hearsay; that history is not asserted as a separate fact here.

description: Myra offers to comb Horse's hair. He accepts; she combs it smooth and ties it into a ponytail with willowbark.
outcome: Horse admires the result and says it is beautiful.
location: Spring at the foot of the butte
evidence_excerpt: She tied it in a massive ponytail with willowbark when she was done. Horse bent over the pool to admire himself. "That's great," he said. "That's really beautiful!"
notes: The location is established on PDF p. 9. No payment or exchange condition is stated.

description: Horse warns Myra that the places she wants to visit are dangerous and says she could be caught there.
outcome: Myra continues to ask about reaching those places.
location: Spring at the foot of the butte
evidence_excerpt: "It's dangerous. Really dangerous. You can't go through —they'd catch you." "I'd just like to know the way."
notes: The danger is Horse's warning. The record does not assert that capture actually happens. The location is established on PDF p. 9.

description: Horse offers to take Myra to the nearest place of the other people. After she agrees and says she cannot run, he helps her onto his shoulders and carries her.
outcome: They begin traveling across the desert together.
location: From the butte across the desert
evidence_excerpt: Horse laughed, a large, cheerful laugh. "Come on," he said, and knelt and held his hands backturned like stirrups for her to mount to his shoulders.
notes: The text describes carrying Myra on his shoulders. Horse's estimate of a return around the following noon is an estimate, not a fixed travel duration.

actor: Old woman at Pygmy Owl camp
description: During Horse and Myra's nighttime stop, an old woman entertains them at her campfire with tales while Myra dozes.
outcome: Myra hears the tales interwoven with her dreams as she dozes and wakes.
evidence_excerpt: an old lady entertained them at her campfire, telling them tales about the ghost of a cricket, about the great invisible people, tales that the child heard interwoven with her own dreams
notes: They also eat and rest at the camp, but the text does not identify who supplies the food. The woman's personal name is unstated.

description: Chickadee offers to accompany Horse and Myra, volunteers to scout, and moves ahead of them.
outcome: Horse says that is great, and she scouts ahead while they continue.
evidence_excerpt: "I'll come along." "That's great," Horse said, thankfully. "I’ll scout," Chickadee said, and off she went, surprisingly fast, ahead of them
notes: The offer is followed by a narrated action. The ranch is identified later on the same page.

description: Myra asks Horse to move closer so she can see the ranch. He goes forward despite being tense.
outcome: Horse moves closer.
location: Sagebrush plain near the ranch fence
evidence_excerpt: "Go closer!" she urged Horse. "I want to see." And as if he owed her obedience, he went forward, tense but unquestioning.
notes: Guidance here means directing movement; it does not imply that the direction is safe or beneficial.

description: Returning from scouting, Chickadee reports that nobody is around but that a fast object she calls a turtle thing is approaching.
outcome: Horse nods and keeps moving forward.
location: Sagebrush plain near the ranch fence
evidence_excerpt: Chickadee came up to them. "Nobody around," she said in her small, dry voice, "but there's one of those fast turtle things coming." Horse nodded, but kept going forward.
notes: The description preserves Chickadee's perspective. No modern vehicle type is assigned.

description: When Myra sees something approaching rapidly, she shouts for Horse to run away. Horse turns and runs with her while Chickadee flies ahead.
outcome: The group moves away from the approaching danger.
location: Near the ranch; desert route away from it
evidence_excerpt: "Run!" she yelled to Horse, "run away! Run!" As if released from bonds he wheeled and ran, flat out, in great reaching strides
notes: The recipient is Horse, who receives the shouted instruction; Myra is also carried away in the resulting action.

description: Chickadee puts heated rocks into a water-filled basket, while Myra adds pounded seeds and stirs.
outcome: They subsequently sit and eat together.
resources: wooden tongs; heated rocks; water; basket; pounded seeds
evidence_excerpt: She took up the wooden tongs, plopped the heated rocks into the water-filled basket with a terrific hiss and steam and loud bubblings. The child sprinkled in the pounded seeds, and stirred.
notes: This records shared work in one scene. Ingredient quantities, cooking duration, and a repeatable recipe are not stated.

description: Chickadee invites Myra to eat, brings out blackberries after their cooking, and shares the meal with her.
outcome: Chickadee and Myra sit on the rug and eat.
evidence_excerpt: Chickadee brought out a basket of fine blackberries. They sat on the newly-shaken-out rug and ate. The child's two-finger scoop technique with mush was now highly refined.
notes: The invitation occurs earlier on the same page. This entry concerns sharing the meal; the preceding entry records the division of cooking work.

description: Responding to Myra's question about Grandmother, Chickadee uses the placement of a fire and the idea of weaving to explain how things belong together.
evidence_excerpt: So we build the fire on sand, on dirt... Things are woven together. So we call the weaver the Grandmother.
notes: This preserves Chickadee's explanation as attributed speech. Her broader account of places and species appears earlier on this page; her speculation about the weaving is qualified with uncertainty.

description: Myra sleeps in a blanket in Chickadee's back yard. After waking, she leaves the blanket folded on Chickadee's bed.
outcome: Myra sleeps deeply and wakes at sunrise.
evidence_excerpt: Lying that night rolled up in a blanket in Chickadee's back yard, the child heard the wind soughing and storming in the cottonwoods down in the draw, and then slept deeply, weary from the long night before.
notes: The text describes the stay and the folded blanket, but does not explicitly narrate Chickadee offering the sleeping place or identify who owns the blanket.

description: Lizard and Beetle sing together in the tobacco patch. Myra hears their song while lying nearby.
outcome: The narration describes Myra feeling rooted in the earth while listening.
location: Wild tobacco patch in the town
evidence_excerpt: Lizard and Beetle were singing some kind of growing song or blessing song, soft and desultory
notes: The narrator qualifies the song as some kind of growing or blessing song. No measured effect on plant growth or routine schedule is established.

description: Coyote enters the marked shack and takes half a smoked salmon. When Myra asks whether this is stealing, Coyote agrees.
outcome: Coyote and Myra eat the salmon beside a dried-up creek.
location: Shack marked fox, private, no trespassing
evidence_excerpt: A sign on the door said: fox. private. no trespassing!— but Coyote pushed it open, and trotted right back out with half a small smoked salmon.
notes: Fox is identified by the sign and is not shown present. The admission of stealing and the shared meal follow on the same page; no permission or later response from Fox is stated.

description: After Myra says she does not want to enter the town, Coyote says they will only approach and look, says they will be careful, and warns about big dogs.
outcome: Coyote leads onward and Myra follows.
location: Approach to the human town between twin hills
evidence_excerpt: Coyote became business-like, responsible. "We're going to be very careful," she announced. "And look out for big dogs, OK? Little dogs I can handle.
notes: Carefulness is promised in dialogue; this does not establish that the visit is safe. Myra initially objects and hangs back.

description: A man approaching with a boy notices Coyote near food and fires a gun at her.
outcome: Coyote flees and Myra escapes from the town with her.
location: Human town near the gas station
evidence_excerpt: the man said, and cocked aimed shot all as Myra screamed and ran against the enormous drowning torrent Coyote fled past her yelling "Get out of here!" She turned and was borne away.
notes: Both man and boy have guns, but only the man is described firing. No gunshot injury is stated.

description: While fleeing the hunter, Coyote tells Myra to leave the town.
outcome: They reach a draw among low hills, out of sight of the town, and recover their breath.
location: Human town near the gas station
evidence_excerpt: Coyote fled past her yelling "Get out of here!" She turned and was borne away.
notes: This is the protective response within the same encounter as the hunter's attack. The outcome is narrated immediately afterward.

description: Myra asks to go home. Coyote refuses for the time being, mocks Myra during their disagreement, and announces that she will remain near the town that night.
outcome: Coyote sits and sings; Myra stays lying nearby and listens.
location: Draw among low hills outside the human town
evidence_excerpt: Look, do what you like, it's a free country. I'm hanging around here tonight. I like the action.
notes: This is a disagreement over where to stay. Coyote tells Myra she may do what she likes; the text does not describe physically forcing her to remain.

description: While listening to Coyote sing after their disagreement, Myra tells Coyote that she loves her.
outcome: Coyote continues singing.
location: Draw among low hills outside the human town
evidence_excerpt: And the child lay listening. "I love you," she said. Coyote went on singing.
notes: No verbal reply or quantified change in their relationship is stated. The category is an editorial grouping for an expression of affection.

description: Myra says the apparent salmon smells funny, like something burned. Coyote dismisses her concern and eats what she calls an offering to herself.
outcome: Coyote becomes severely ill after eating.
location: Near a fence outside the human town
evidence_excerpt: The child looked dubiously at the salmon. "It smells funny." "How funny?" "Like burned." "It's smoked, stupid! Come on."
notes: The offering is Coyote's interpretation. Page 16 identifies a poisoned lamb carcass where the salmon had appeared; the person who placed it is not identified.

description: Myra tries to hold Coyote through her spasms and continues holding her warm body in the hope that she will recover.
outcome: Coyote's body becomes cold; Myra recognizes that she has died.
location: Near a fence outside the human town
evidence_excerpt: The child scrambled back and held the body as it spasmed again, twitched, quivered, went still. By moonrise Coyote was cold.
notes: The recognition of death continues at the start of page 16. Recovery is Myra's hope, not the outcome.

description: Myra digs a shallow pit, carries Coyote's body into it, covers her with a bandanna, and heaps sand, rocks, and plants over the body.
outcome: Coyote's body is buried.
location: Stony sand in the draw outside the human town
resources: blue and white bandanna; sand; rocks; sagebrush; tumbleweed
evidence_excerpt: She carried the small corpse to the pit, laid it down, and covered it with her blue and white bandanna. It was not large enough; the four stiff paws stuck out.
notes: The narration contrasts Myra's people's burial practice with Coyote's people's practice. Do not treat this act as a universal community custom.

description: Chickadee meets Myra on the second evening north of Horse Butte and brings her into Grandmother's house.
outcome: Myra and Chickadee meet Grandmother at her loom.
location: North of Horse Butte; Grandmother's underground house
evidence_excerpt: It was Chickadee who met her, on the second evening north of Horse Butte. "I didn't cry," the child said. "None of us do," said Chickadee. "Come with me this way now. Come into Grandmother's house."
notes: The movement into the house follows the invitation in the narration.

description: Grandmother advises Myra to return to her own people, asks about her father, and tells her that people have kept searching for her.
outcome: After the conversation, Myra thanks Grandmother and starts up the slope toward the next day.
evidence_excerpt: If you go back now, you can still live with them. Isn't your father there?" The child nodded. "They've been looking for you."
notes: The search is reported by Grandmother. Myra's departure is on page 17; an arrival or reunion with her father is not narrated.

description: Grandmother reassures Myra that she can live well among her people and says she will remain present in Myra's dreams, ideas, and surroundings.
evidence_excerpt: Don't be afraid. You can live well there. I'll be there too, you know. In your dreams, in your ideas, in dark comers in the basement.
notes: This is reassurance and a statement about future presence; its later fulfillment is not shown. The excerpt retains the PDF extraction's word 'comers'.

description: Chickadee says she will visit Myra and asks Myra to make gardens for her.
evidence_excerpt: "I'll come around," Chickadee said. "Make gardens for me."
notes: A future visit is promised and gardens are requested. The passage does not show a garden being made or specify plants, timing, or rewards.
